label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
read: RC2 70-page edition, draft: manuscript/rc2/70/ (17 files) and its 55-page PDF built at 893dadaf
where_i_skimmed_or_stopped: 07 the rhythm and 08 the plumbing: the hour-by-hour chart is good, but the prose around it repeats the check and the first-night banner story already told in chapter 3
10 the last ten minutes: a long minute-by-minute account of a lock that never turned; I wanted the lesson sooner
14 the second factory: the cast roll-call and the Web Summit plan read as promise, not evidence; I skimmed the plan
15 principles: it only restates chapters 3 to 12, so I read it as a recap and skipped
first_thing_i_would_do: Write one page of rules for a single researcher-checker agent that may write only a claims register, then have it grade every number in my first story before I sign.
price: about 12 to 15 pounds as a short practical book; I would pay more only if the figures were all drawn and the newsroom case were addressed
why: The register of claims, the reviewer that is honestly called a second reading and not a wall, and the failures left in are exactly what I look for in a method I could put my name on. But the book is the story of a talk factory, not a newsroom, and I have to translate every role myself. Too many pictures are still boxes in this draft, and my deal breaker is only half answered: the editor signs in the book's own factory, but on the talk's day he mostly pressed a hold and gave feedback, and only eight of ten policies were agreed. I am left unsure whether signing is a control or a courtesy.

by_chapter.why: Strong opening, and the voice-note quotes are honest and vivid. The loop idea (see, ask, see again) is clear. It is about slides, not stories, so I translate. The 18:25 to 18:37 round trip is the kind of traced number I trust.
by_chapter.quote: I was the bit in between.

by_chapter.why: Seven stops is a catalogue and most of the pictures are still 'Figure to come'. The 162 against 163 counter note is the one moment I love: the book follows the register and says why.
by_chapter.quote: The page has a counter. I have a register. When they differ, the book uses mine and says why.

by_chapter.why: The first page of rules, the reality file and the 'None yet' corrections file are the most copyable things in the book. The shop-owner example makes it startlingly practical.
by_chapter.quote: A thing not listed here does not exist, whatever a brief or an article says.

by_chapter.why: Roles as readable pages, each with the mistake behind its rule. The researcher who cannot change a slide is exactly the fact-checker I want. The scope-is-a-setting line is honest. Security never staffed is a good admission.
by_chapter.quote: A scope is a setting, not a boundary

by_chapter.why: One wake walked step by step, including a partial verdict and a reviewer finding, is the best chapter for understanding the method. Seeing the agent not round itself up convinces me more than any claim.
by_chapter.quote: a second reading, not a second identity.

by_chapter.why: Mail, board and notes in commits are concrete and cheap to copy. The researcher arguing with its reviewer and the record keeping both halves shows the control working. A folder of requests is something I would do on day one.
by_chapter.quote: If it is not in a file, it did not happen.

by_chapter.why: The chart is the best picture in the book. The rest overlaps with 06 and with the later 'sessions end'. The '@' complaint recurs three times and begins to feel like filler.
by_chapter.quote: Nobody was watching, and they argued, sent work back, owned their mistakes and kept the books.

by_chapter.why: The register chapter is the one I was waiting for: 320 claims, 210 held, 55 in part, 52 unchecked, three did not hold, and none said on stage. The corrections file nobody used is a useful confession. I want this earlier in the book.
by_chapter.quote: Gaps are allowed. Hiding them is not.

by_chapter.why: The objection kept is the one scene that answers my rubber-stamp worry: the researcher says a claim does not hold, the editor keeps it anyway, and both are recorded. Port, not rebuild is a sound economic point. The relayed word refused is good.
by_chapter.quote: Then it goes to the editor, as the strongest objection to his own part one. Not buried.

by_chapter.why: The minute-by-minute is vivid, but it narrates a failed lock at length. The hold file as a page is good, and the line 'I could keep going. That is exactly why I am stopping.' is the one to keep.
by_chapter.quote: I could keep going. That is exactly why I am stopping.

by_chapter.why: The failures at full size are why I would trust the rest. Three different reasons for the stop, all kept as said, and the stale $17.4M against $19.5M is a small, true error shown with its source. The one place the book proves it will not tidy itself.
by_chapter.quote: The lesson for your first week: when you freeze something, write down what is waiting to go in when you unfreeze it.

by_chapter.why: The brake as one state machine is clear and the honest answer to my 'where would I not trust it' question: reviewers share the same reach and the outside reviewer was never there. The unswitched control point is true of every newsroom I know. The relayed-word refusal is credible.
by_chapter.quote: Most controls do not fail because someone defeats them. They fail because nobody gets round to switching them on.

by_chapter.why: Session versus member, and the handover read out, are directly useful if my own agent account runs out. Key handling described and not shown is right.
by_chapter.quote: A member of the team is a role

by_chapter.why: Useful for the two failures kept (the corrected brake line, the evening lost to the limit). The cast roll-call and the third factory are plan, not record, and I stopped trusting them for that reason.
by_chapter.quote: Nothing was harmed and nothing is half-done.

by_chapter.why: Six principles with where each came from. A good reference card, but it adds nothing new if I have read the book; it could be a single page.
by_chapter.quote: I do not trust principles that arrive without a story.

by_chapter.why: The five steps plus the checklist is what I would actually use. The $20 a month line is sourced to a date, which I note with approval. I still need a newsroom example, and a 'which first role' answer: the book says start with one conductor, but I would start with the checker.
by_chapter.quote: You do not need my nine. You need one.

by_chapter.why: Useful as a glossary. 'Wake' and 'hold' are the words I most needed pinned down. It should sit nearer the front for a newcomer.

p40: the cards at the top are fine but the text under them is dense

p46: the second factory cast list, many one-line speeches in a row
p50: principles, six similar blocks in a row with no visual break
best_line: Nobody needs permission to stop. Everybody needs his to start again.
worst_moment: Chapter 2 and chapter 12 each depend on boxes that read 'Figure to come' in a book about showing; in the second half there is a run of boxes (pages 41 to 43, 45, 51, 54) where the key picture of the argument is missing and a caption stands in for it.
versus_the_thirty: The seventy adds what I most want: the single walked-through wake (05), the register and the unused corrections file (08), the objection the editor kept (09), the full failures (11) and the honest containment chapter (12). Those turn a good story into a method I can check. It also adds repetition (07 and 08 retell the first-night banner and the '@' note), a catalogue tour, and plan material in 14. I would take the seventy for the register, wake and failures chapters, and want it trimmed by about ten pages.
top_three_changes: Draw the missing pictures, first the wake record page (p21), the register bar (p30) and the dashboard (p11); a book about reading the record should show a record.

Add one newsroom path to chapter 16 (researcher-checker first, a story brief, the editor signs each piece) and say plainly what the editor's signature checks, with an example of an editor who disagreed or rejected something, so signing reads as control and not as ceremony.
Cut or merge the repeats: fold 15 into a one-page card, trim 07 and 08 where they retell chapter 3, shorten 10, and move the register (08) and the words (17) nearer the front.
notes: Persona note: I am exacting about sources, so I checked for numbers without a register. Every number I read points back to the register or a dated record, which is why I stayed; the editor's own 95% accounts being kept in three versions is exactly the right instinct. My doubt is that the editor's role in the talk factory reads as feedback giver and brake puller, not as the signature on each output. A deal breaker for me is an editor who only rubber-stamps, and the book does not yet show a signature declined. Also: the book calls the stop-line check 'catches mistakes, not a steered agent', which I would use as a line for my own readers.
